w: 1 Cairo RT1, RT2, RT3: how much root coverage to expect A professor's hint · 6 questions in the bank Know this Cairo: RT1 (no interproximal loss) about 100% coverage; RT2 (interproximal CAL less than or equal to buccal) partial, about 50-60%, up to the interproximal level; RT3 (interproximal greater) none. RT2: recession with loss of interproximal attachment, where the interproximal CAL (from the interproximal CEJ to the depth of the interproximal sulcus or pocket) is less than or equal to the buccal CAL (from the buccal CEJ to the depth of the buccal sulcus or pocket). You can see the CEJ interproximally. Expect partial root coverage, about 50 to 60% in cases like his: at best up to the level of the interproximal attachment on either side. The tissue can't be pulled any higher, because there is no framework and no blood supply interproximally to hold it there ("if we know how to fix this, we could ... cure everybody from periodontitis"). 2 Which graft: a covered graft is a CTG, under a coronally advanced flap A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Root coverage with a CTG or an ADM: the flap is advanced coronally, tension free, over the graft. The two main sources in the US are the patient's own tissue, an autograft, and donor tissue from a tissue bank, an allograft; there are others (bovine, porcine). The most common graft comes from the palate (or the tuberosity), because the palate is orthokeratinized: its tissue "carries that information of keratinization with it" to the recipient site. Palatal connective tissue induces epithelial differentiation and keratinization. From the palate you take either a free gingival graft (FGG), the epithelium together with the lamina propria (the connective tissue) under it in one piece, or a subepithelial connective tissue graft (SCTG, or CTG), the connective tissue without the epithelium. His case: recession on #10 and #11 (part of a composite filling was removed first). A trapezoidal flap, raised partial thickness to keep some of the periosteum, exposed the roots; the graft size was planned (a template helps) and a CTG harvested from the palate, its epithelium removed. The graft was placed and sutured, then the flap was advanced coronally over it, tension free, so it holds its coronal position covering the recessions and the graft completely. At about four weeks the coverage was good, and coverage that looks like this early usually holds. The profile view shows the other gain: much thicker tissue over the roots, a thick phenotype "that by definition would resist much better" further recession. "We always do a coronally advanced flap if we're trying to cover the graft." 3 Inflammation causes recession; the factors only predispose A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this Inflammation causes recession, by either pathway (brushing trauma or plaque). Thin phenotype, brushing, dehiscences, orthodontics, margins, the frenum and smokeless tobacco only predispose. Two mechanisms (from Zucchelli's textbook). Toothbrushing trauma, especially on thin tissue: the epithelium is abraded, the connective tissue under it responds with inflammation, an ulcer forms at the surface, and with continued trauma the margin recedes. Plaque-related: the same process as periodontitis (plaque in the sulcus with poor hygiene, apical and lateral migration of the junctional epithelium, loss of attachment), here on a local scale on a thin phenotype. "The key word here is inflammation": it is what actually causes recession, and the factors above are predisposing factors that make it happen. 4 Keratinized gingiva: the 2 mm rule, and an FGG left exposed to create it A professor's hint · 5 questions in the bank Know this With good plaque control KG isn't essential; with suboptimal plaque control at least 2 mm is needed to prevent attachment loss. To create KG, use an FGG left exposed with an apically positioned flap. A CTG covered by mucosa gains no KG. Is keratinized gingiva needed? A zone of attached gingiva is, of and by itself, not essential for keeping periodontal health and attachment, when dental plaque is controlled and there are no other traumatic factors (Kennedy and colleagues, 1985; Scheyer and colleagues, the AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). If plaque control is suboptimal, at least 2 mm of KG is needed to prevent attachment loss. Many patients don't have optimal plaque control, so a tooth with less than 2 mm of KG is likely prone to recession. That doesn't mean every such tooth needs a graft: it is case by case. Not every patient lacking KG has recession, but lacking it predisposes to it, while a thick phenotype with a wide band of KG resists it. His patient had an RT2 recession on a sensitive tooth with no KG: the site was a plaque trap, chronically irritating the margin and leading to more recession. The goal was to change the quality of the tissue, creating a band of KG; root coverage would be a bonus. A CTG under a coronally advanced flap wouldn't do it: covering the graft with the only tissue there, alveolar mucosa, gains no keratinized gingiva, because mucosa doesn't become keratinized just because it covers a graft. So he used a free gingival graft with an apically positioned flap: a trapezoidal flap (a horizontal incision and two vertical ones) placed apically, and an FGG from the palate, with its epithelium, left exposed so it heals into a band of KG, bringing its own determination to keratinize. Covering it with the flap would deny it that. The palate heals by secondary intention. The graft is held only by sutures, so patients are told not to pull the lip down to look at it every day, to keep a soft diet and not to brush the area while it heals. At three months there was a good band of KG where there had been none, blending with the neighboring tissue (bigger on the apical side), and partial root coverage, as expected for RT2. Her sensitivity was gone, the site was easier to clean and less of a plaque trap, and the phenotype was thicker and more protective. 5 The acellular dermal matrix: what it is, when, and why it's covered Hint + review guide · 6 questions in the bank Know this An acellular dermal matrix has no cells or blood supply: always fully covered; remodeled and replaced by the patient's tissue; best for many teeth at once. Treating many teeth from the palate means a large, invasive harvest. When you can avoid that, use a soft tissue allograft: donated human dermis, usually from cadavers, processed to remove the epidermis, the hair follicles and the existing cells. What is left, the acellular dermal matrix (ADM, or ADMA; AlloDerm is one), is a matrix of collagen, elastic and reticular fibers with no cells. It wasn't designed for dentistry: it has been used since 1995 for burns, head and neck reconstruction, urology (bladder slings, pelvic floor reconstruction), orthopedics (rotator cuff repair, periosteal replacement) and hernia repair, and in dentistry since 1997, now in dental sizes. It is the most common soft tissue allograft (exam-review guide). Advantages (slide): it eliminates the need for a donor site; increases patient acceptance (no surgery on the roof of the mouth); decreases surgical time; treats multiple defects in one procedure ("quote-unquote unlimited quantities"); achieves esthetic results comparable or superior to autogenous tissue; and is easy to use. Disadvantages (recording): it is "more or less a dead piece of skin" with nothing to contribute to the healing, "like a band-aid." So it must be fully covered by the flap, because it heals poorly left exposed without a blood supply. Over time it is remodeled and replaced by the patient's own tissue (histology shows this). In a more demanding site it can't give the same benefit as autogenous tissue; the exam-review guide's summary is that allografts don't work as well as autografts but have many advantages. 6 Untreated recession progresses; why treat it A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Know this Chambrone and Tatakis (2016): untreated recession progresses, so a recession that doesn't hurt still needs a decision. Exposed roots and lost tissue raise the likelihood of (1) dentinal hypersensitivity, (2) soft tissue discomfort (thin tissue with little keratinized gingiva can hurt to brush), (3) root surface caries, (4) esthetic concerns, (5) interference with adequate mechanical plaque control, and (6) greater susceptibility to inflammatory insult. And recession doesn't sit still: a systematic review (Chambrone and Tatakis, 2016) found that untreated recession defects continue to progress, the margin moving further apical. So "let's just monitor it" because it doesn't hurt, isn't sensitive and isn't in the esthetic zone doesn't mean it will stay the same. Apart from RT3, recession should be considered for treatment when indicated. (Restorative ways to treat recession are for next year's course; this session is about soft tissue grafting.) 7 Thin vs thick phenotype: the probe test and recession risk A professor's hint · 3 questions in the bank Why it matters: a thin phenotype is predisposed to recession, and recession that is already there tends to progress on it, while a thick phenotype resists it. His example: a young patient about to start orthodontics had a thin phenotype over his incisors, so thin you could see the roots. Orthodontic movement, then years of toothbrushing on top of it, would put him at risk of recession he didn't have yet. So before the orthodontics the phenotype was changed from thin to thick: a trapezoidal, full-thickness flap, a connective tissue graft from the palate sutured over the two central incisors (the teeth most at risk), and the flap put back over the graft to cover it completely. At two weeks the tissue was already thicker, and he was cleared for orthodontics with less risk of recession. 8 Altered passive eruption: the types and their crown lengthening Review guide + slides · 6 questions in the bank The treatment is crown lengthening, matched to the type: a gingivectomy only in Type 1A; an apically positioned flap in Type 2A; an apically positioned flap plus osseous surgery in Types 1B and 2B. The logic behind the rule: in a B type the bone itself sits too close to the CEJ, so the bone has to be moved, whatever the gingiva; in Type 2 the band of gingiva is only of normal width, so cutting gingiva away would cost keratinized gingiva, and the flap moves the band apically instead. Only Type 1A has both extra gingiva and room above the bone. 9 Excessive gingival display: the cause from the findings, and its treatment Review guide + slides · 8 questions in the bank The possible etiologies, each with the finding that points to it on the slides: short clinical crowns (altered passive eruption), with abnormal tooth dimensions and proportions and gingival line asymmetries; vertical maxillary excess, with an increased lower facial third; a short upper lip, with a lip length under 20 mm; a hypermobile upper lip, with lip mobility over 8 mm; or a combination of these. The slide's table: altered passive eruption, crown lengthening and restorative therapy; vertical maxillary excess, orthodontics and orthognathic surgery, and periodontics may be required to correct the gingival display; a hypermobile upper lip, lip repositioning surgery or Botox may reduce the display; a short upper lip, no good options. When several factors are present, a combination of therapies may be considered. 10 Pseudopockets and drug-induced enlargement Review guide · 3 questions in the bank The slides give four etiologies of gingival excess, each with its treatment. 1. Pseudopocket: gingivitis, the gingiva swollen coronally so the probing depth grows without attachment loss. Treatment: improved oral hygiene measures and scaling. 2. Gingival enlargement: gingival diseases modified by medications, phenytoin, calcium channel blockers and cyclosporine. Treatment: gingivectomy, improved oral hygiene and possibly a change of the contributing medication. 3. Inconsistent gingival margins: discrepant gingival margins of contralateral teeth, a gingival line discrepancy. Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap. 4. Excessive gingival display, a "gummy smile." Treatment: gingivectomy or an apically positioned flap, but first find its cause, because it has several. 11 Esthetic norms: the lip, the gingival line, the golden proportion Review guide · 4 questions in the bank His checklist on the slides. Facial symmetry: the facial thirds, and the facial midline against the dental midline; an increased lower facial third suggests vertical maxillary excess. Smile line (lip line): high, medium or low. Incisal line: it should be consonant with the lower lip. Upper lip, height and mobility: 20-22 mm for women, 22-24 mm for men, and normal lip mobility is 6-8 mm, measured with a caliper at rest and in a full smile. Gingival line: the central incisors and canines at the same level, and the lateral incisors 1 mm coronal to them. Tooth shape, dimensions and proportions: the golden proportion, which the slides show in nature, art and architecture. Seen from the front, the central incisor is about 1.618 times as wide as the lateral, and the lateral 1.618 times the visible part of the canine, so centrals, laterals and canines show at about 1.618 : 1 : 0.618 (the exam-review guide rounds it to 1.6, 1 and 0.6 for half the canine). On the slide a 9 mm central goes with a 5.56 mm lateral and 3.44 mm of canine. 12 The palate: its layers, the greater palatine bundle, the high vault Review guide · 3 questions in the bank The anatomy to stay away from is the greater palatine artery and nerve, the neurovascular bundle. On the slide it runs about 7 mm from the CEJ in a shallow palate, 12 mm in an average palate and 17 mm in a high palate. So a high, deep palatal vault gives the most room for error when harvesting (the exam-review guide's point). There are guidelines for which area to harvest from (premolar, molar) and how far up the palate to go. Also flagged in class RT3 is the one type not to graft for root coverage; the other types should be considered for treatment when indicated. Covered graft = CTG (connective tissue only). Exposed graft = FGG (epithelium plus lamina propria). Probe visible through the tissue = thin (1 mm or less), prone to recession; not visible = thick (more than 1 mm). Of the traumatic factors (brushing, flossing, habits, foreign objects, caustic medicaments), toothbrushing is the most common. You can skip Restorative treatment of recession is next year's course; this session tests soft tissue grafting.
